questions.q: Why can't fuzz or invariant tests catch a silent gas cost regression?
options: They can — gas snapshotting is redundant
Because the contract still behaves correctly; it's just more expensive, and correctness tests only check behavior
Because fuzz tests don't run on real contracts
Because gas cost is random and can't be tested
questions.explain: A gas regression doesn't break correctness — the contract still returns the right results — so correctness-focused tests have no reason to fail.

options: A screenshot of the terminal
A .gas-snapshot file recording every test's gas usage as a committed baseline
A deployment transaction
A list of all contract addresses
questions.explain: forge snapshot runs the test suite and writes each test's gas usage into .gas-snapshot, which gets committed as the baseline to compare future runs against.

questions.q: For a fuzz test, what does the .gas-snapshot file record instead of a single gas number?
options: Only the highest gas value seen across all runs
The mean (μ) and median (~) gas usage across all fuzz runs
The gas cost of the first run only
Nothing — fuzz tests are excluded from snapshots
questions.explain: Since a fuzz test's gas cost varies by input, the snapshot records both the mean and median across all runs rather than one number.

questions.q: Which flag belongs in a CI pipeline to fail the build on a gas regression?
options: forge snapshot --init
forge snapshot --check
forge snapshot --reset
forge snapshot --silent
questions.explain: forge snapshot --check exits with an error if any test now uses more gas than the committed baseline, making it suitable as a CI gate.

questions.q: What's the correct workflow when a gas increase is intentional (e.g. trading gas for a needed safety check)?
options: Ignore the --check failure permanently
Delete the .gas-snapshot file entirely
Regenerate the snapshot with forge snapshot and commit the updated .gas-snapshot so the change is visible in the PR diff
Lower the compiler optimization setting instead
questions.explain: Deliberately regenerating and committing the snapshot makes the gas change a reviewable part of the PR, rather than a silent creep or a permanently blocked CI check.
